beaches.name: Praia do Pinhão
beaches.vibeLine: Lagos' best-kept secret — a tiny sheltered cove steps from town that most people walk right past.
beaches.bestTime: Flexible — it's rarely crowded even in summer. Morning sun hits the beach directly, afternoon brings natural shade from the cliffs. Off-season you'll likely have it to yourself.
beaches.parking: Use the paid car park near Praia Dona Ana (5 min walk along the cliff path). Don't waste time looking for closer options — there aren't any.
beaches.personalTake: This is my go-to when I want a quick swim without the circus. While everyone fights for space at Dona Ana, I walk five minutes further and have a cove practically to myself. The tunnel connecting to the second beach section is a fun surprise at low tide.
beaches.skipIf: You need facilities, shade umbrellas, or flat easy access. The narrow staircase between rocks isn't signposted — that's the point.

beaches.name: Praia do Carvalho
beaches.vibeLine: Small beach accessed through a hand-carved tunnel in the cliff. Feels like discovering something.
beaches.bestTime: Arrive before 9:30am in summer. After 11am, the small beach fills completely. Off-season is magic — often empty.
beaches.parking: Small dirt lot at the top. Gets full fast. No nearby alternatives — if it's full, you're out of luck.
beaches.personalTake: One of my favourites for the sense of discovery. The tunnel alone is worth the visit — look for fossils in the walls as you pass through. But manage expectations — it's tiny. Stay on the left side in the afternoon to keep the sun.
beaches.skipIf: You need shade, facilities, or space. Families with very young kids will find the access tricky. Don't sit near the cliff base — rockfall is real.

beaches.name: Praia da Ilha da Fuseta
beaches.vibeLine: A desert island in the Ria Formosa that locals treat as their private paradise. The ferry ride is half the fun.
beaches.bestTime: Any time works — even August, the deserted stretches stay deserted. Ferries run every 10 minutes in summer (€2 return). Walk east for 20 minutes and you'll feel like Robinson Crusoe.
beaches.parking: Park in Fuseta marina/village. Then it's all about the ferry.
beaches.personalTake: This is the beach I send friends to when they want the 'real' Algarve. The main landing area has some people, but walk east along the sand for 20 minutes and it's just you, the birds, and the Atlantic. Bring snorkelling gear — the clear water over the sandbars is full of life. After, eat in Fuseta village — it's a working fishing town with honest restaurants.
beaches.skipIf: You don't want to take a ferry, or you need beach bars and loungers. This is bring-everything territory.

beaches.name: Praia de Albandeira
beaches.vibeLine: A dramatic natural rock arch, crystal-clear swimming, and somehow half the tourists don't know it exists.
beaches.bestTime: Before 10am in summer for parking. Spring and autumn are perfect — warm enough to swim, empty enough to breathe.
beaches.parking: Small lot at the clifftop. Limited spaces — this is an early-bird beach. No alternatives nearby.
beaches.personalTake: Albandeira is what Marinha would be if Instagram hadn't found it. The natural arch is just as spectacular, the water is just as clear, but you're not fighting for towel space. I always combine it with Marinha for a two-beach day — they're 10 minutes apart by car. The cliff stairs can be slippery when wet, so wear proper shoes.
beaches.skipIf: You need facilities of any kind — there's nothing here. The steep wooden stairs are not mobility-friendly.

beaches.name: Praia do Paraíso
beaches.vibeLine: Tiny cliff paradise with 130 steps down and turquoise water that earns its name.
beaches.bestTime: Check tide times — at high tide there's almost no sand. Morning for swimming, but the sunset view from the clifftop above is far better than from below.
beaches.parking: Free parking along Estrada do Paraíso. Limited spaces but manageable outside peak summer weekends.
beaches.personalTake: The 130 steps down are a natural crowd filter — most people give up and go to Carvoeiro instead. Your reward is turquoise water in a cliff amphitheatre that feels private. The water shoes are non-negotiable though — the shallows are rocky. After the climb back up, the Mar d'Fora restaurant at the clifftop does excellent drinks with a view.
beaches.skipIf: High tide days (check before going). Mobility issues — 130 steep steps is no joke, and you have to climb back up.

beaches.name: Praia do Camilo
beaches.vibeLine: 200 steep wooden steps to a cliff-framed double cove — the most photographed staircase in the Algarve, and one of the most beautiful beaches in Europe.
beaches.bestTime: Before 9am in summer or you'll queue on the staircase itself. Off-season (Oct-Apr) is perfect — fewer people, great light. Low tide connects the two coves via a natural rock tunnel.
beaches.parking: Very limited along the road above. Most people park at Dona Ana (5 min walk) or Ponta da Piedade (10 min walk). Don't waste 30 minutes circling for a closer spot.
beaches.personalTake: Yes, it's famous. Yes, every influencer has the same staircase photo. But stand at the bottom looking up at those golden cliffs framing turquoise water, and you'll understand why. The secret is the rock tunnel at low tide connecting to a second, emptier cove. Combine with Ponta da Piedade clifftop walk — they're neighbours. Just accept the 200 steps back up.
beaches.skipIf: You hate stairs or crowds. July-August midday is genuinely unpleasant — the small beach is standing room only. Mobility issues make this a no-go.

beaches.name: Praia do Vale de Centeanes
beaches.vibeLine: A cliff-backed cove between Carvoeiro and Benagil that's the launching point for the famous cave — but a destination beach in its own right.
beaches.bestTime: Arrive before 10am in summer. The beach faces south so it gets sun all day. Late afternoon is golden hour magic with the cliffs glowing orange.
beaches.parking: Free parking lot at the top of the cliff. Fills fast in summer — arrive early. The wooden boardwalk down to the beach is steep but manageable.
beaches.personalTake: Most people treat Vale de Centeanes as a kayak departure point for Benagil Cave and miss the beach itself. That's their loss. The cliff amphitheatre creates a sheltered swimming pool, the restaurant at the top is solid, and the coastal walk east towards Benagil along the clifftops is one of the best short hikes in the Algarve. If you're kayaking to Benagil, launching from here is calmer than from Benagil beach itself.
beaches.skipIf: You need a big sandy stretch — this is a compact cove. The access stairs are steep and not ideal for very young children or mobility issues.

beaches.name: Praia dos Caneiros
beaches.vibeLine: Upscale beach vibes with a famous cliff restaurant, and a hidden beach at low tide that most people never find.
beaches.bestTime: Arrive before 10am in summer for parking. The real move: check tide times and explore Praia do Torrado at low tide — walk around the western cliff to find it.
beaches.parking: Small free car park next to the beach. Fills fast in summer. If full, park further back and walk — don't circle the lot hoping.
beaches.personalTake: Caneiros is two beaches in one. The main beach is lovely — Blue Flag water, dramatic offshore rocks, and Rei das Praias restaurant perched on stilts above the sand (book a sunset window table weeks in advance). But the real secret is Praia do Torrado at low tide — walk around the western cliff and you'll find a hidden cove that feels like it shouldn't exist.
beaches.skipIf: You're on a tight budget — the restaurant is pricey and there's no cheap alternative nearby. Don't sit under the cliffs despite the tempting shade — rockfall signs are there for a reason.

beaches.name: Praia Dona Ana
beaches.vibeLine: Lagos' postcard beach — golden cliffs, turquoise water, and the most facilities of any cove on the south coast. Beautiful, but no secret.
beaches.bestTime: Before 10am or after 5pm in summer. The beach is south-facing so it gets sun all day. Off-season it's genuinely lovely — warm enough to sit, empty enough to enjoy.
beaches.parking: Large paid car park directly above the beach (€1/hour). One of the few Lagos beaches with reliable parking. The walk down is short and manageable.
beaches.personalTake: Dona Ana is the most famous beach in Lagos and I'm including it because a guide without it would feel incomplete — but I won't pretend it's a hidden gem. It's beautiful, the facilities are excellent, and the cliffs are genuinely spectacular. Just manage your expectations in summer — this is not a peaceful escape, it's a proper beach experience. For the hidden alternative, walk 5 minutes south to Praia do Pinhão.
beaches.skipIf: You want solitude. In July-August it's packed by 11am. The beach isn't huge and it can feel claustrophobic at peak times.

beaches.name: Praia da Luz
beaches.vibeLine: Family beach with character — the Black Rock formation gives it a personality most resort beaches lack.
beaches.bestTime: The eastern end near Rocha Negra is always less crowded. Low tide unlocks hidden coves and the best rock pools on the western side. Summer means lifeguards and full facilities.
beaches.parking: Main Luz beach parking. For the hidden coves at the western end, it's a 15-minute walk from the car park.
beaches.personalTake: Luz gets overlooked because Lagos steals all the attention, but families are better off here. The village is calmer, the beach is spacious, and the Rocha Negra gives kids something to explore beyond sandcastles. At low tide, the western coves have rock pools teeming with life. If you're feeling adventurous, hike up the Black Rock at sunset — the views are incredible.
beaches.skipIf: You want dramatic cliff scenery (it's pretty but not Ponta da Piedade). You're looking for nightlife — Luz is quiet after dark.

beaches.name: Praia da Coelha
beaches.vibeLine: A local favourite hiding in plain sight near Albufeira — the 400-metre walk through olive trees keeps the crowds away.
beaches.bestTime: Weekdays are significantly quieter. The walk from the car park is shaded and pleasant, so even midday arrivals are fine. Summer has lifeguards and the beach restaurant opens.
beaches.parking: Car park about 400m from the beach. The walk through olive and carob trees is actually lovely — don't see it as a negative.
beaches.personalTake: This is my answer when people say 'we're staying near Albufeira but want a nice beach.' The 400-metre walk acts as a natural filter — tourist buses don't come here. There's a distinctive sea arch, the water is absurdly clear, and the beach restaurant serves genuinely good fresh fish. It never feels crowded, even when Albufeira's main beaches are packed to the walls.
beaches.skipIf: You need direct car-to-sand access (400m walk through olive trees required). August weekends can get busy despite the walk — try weekday mornings instead. The beach faces south-southwest so you lose sun earlier than east-facing beaches.

beaches.name: Praia de Salema
beaches.vibeLine: An authentic fishing village beach with 150-million-year-old dinosaur footprints — yes, really.
beaches.bestTime: Low tide is essential for the dinosaur footprints on the western cliffs. The eastern end is always quieter. Saturday mornings combine well with the village market.
beaches.parking: 60-space car park directly behind the beach. Fills quickly in summer — larger overflow parking 5 minutes uphill.
beaches.personalTake: Salema is what the Algarve felt like 20 years ago. Fishing boats still line the beach, the village has real character, and then there are the dinosaur footprints — 150 million years old, just sitting there on the rocks at low tide. Rick Steves called it one of Europe's most enjoyable beaches, and for once I agree with a guidebook. Água na Boca in the village is excellent for dinner after.
beaches.skipIf: You want resort amenities or beach clubs. Salema is beautifully simple — that's the whole point.

beaches.name: Praia da Falésia
beaches.vibeLine: Six kilometres of golden sand beneath 42-metre cliffs that look like they belong in Utah. Walk 100 metres from the stairs and you'll have it to yourself.
beaches.bestTime: The trick: walk 100m from any access point and the crowds vanish. Three access points — Olhos de Água (west), Acoteias (central, most popular), and Vilamoura/Alfamar (east, easiest access, no steep stairs).
beaches.parking: Three options: Olhos de Água (small, 43 spaces), Acoteias (larger), Vilamoura/Alfamar (large, paid at €2.80/hour). Arrive before 10am in summer at Acoteias.
beaches.personalTake: TripAdvisor ranked it #5 in the world, and honestly? It deserves it. The red, orange, and white cliffs are 5-23 million years old and more dramatic than any photo suggests. The genius of Falésia is that it's 6km long — the crowds cluster near the stairs, but a short walk gives you empty stretches that feel like a private beach. The cliff-top trail connecting all three access points is one of the best coastal walks in the Algarve. Stay well clear of the cliff base though — erosion is constant.
beaches.skipIf: You want intimate cove vibes — this is a big, wide beach. The Vilamoura end has trendy beach clubs if that's your thing; if it's not, head to the quieter Olhos de Água end.

beaches.name: Praia da Ingrina
beaches.vibeLine: A sheltered shell-shaped cove near Sagres where the water is always calm and always clear. Perfect for kids and snorkellers.
beaches.bestTime: The sheltered position means calm water even when nearby beaches have waves. September is best — water's been warming all summer and the crowds are gone.
beaches.parking: Small free lot above the beach. Fills on summer weekends — arrive before 10am. Manageable outside peak times.
beaches.personalTake: When people near Sagres ask where to take their kids, I send them here. The cove shape creates a natural swimming pool — calm, clear, and shallow enough for small children. Bring your own snorkelling gear (no rentals) and explore the natural rock pier extending into the sea. The restaurant does excellent grilled fish. Combine with nearby Praia do Zavial for a full day of contrasting beaches — calm family cove, then wild surf.
beaches.skipIf: You want waves or a big sandy beach. Ingrina is small and sheltered — that's the whole appeal.

beaches.name: Praia do Castelejo
beaches.vibeLine: The Financial Times called it 'a perfect beach.' Towering 156-metre dark cliffs, wild Atlantic, and a fog that appears from nowhere.
beaches.bestTime: Check the forecast — Castelejo has its own microclimate that brings fog even when everywhere else is sunny. When it's clear, any time works — it rarely gets crowded. Connects to Cordoama at low tide.
beaches.parking: Large free parking directly above the beach. Always space available. The road getting here is narrow and winding — allow extra time.
beaches.personalTake: Castelejo is where I go to remember why the Algarve isn't just another beach destination. The cliffs are the tallest on the entire coast — 156 metres of dark schist that make you feel tiny. The restaurant is surprisingly good (octopus is the star), and the atmospheric fog that rolls in unannounced adds a drama you won't find on the south coast. Walk to Cordoama at low tide for an extended experience, but watch the tides carefully.
beaches.skipIf: You want guaranteed sunshine — the fog is unpredictable. Families wanting calm swimming — this is Atlantic surf territory. The drive from the south coast takes 30+ minutes on winding roads.

beaches.name: Praia da Cordoama
beaches.vibeLine: Over a kilometre of empty sand where you can always — always — find parking. The antidote to everything overcrowded.
beaches.bestTime: Mid to high tide for the best surf. Low tide gets dumpy. Unlike every other Algarve beach, parking is always available here, even on peak summer weekends.
beaches.parking: Free parking right behind the beach. Always space available — I'm not exaggerating. Paved lot plus overflow area.
beaches.personalTake: Cordoama is the beach I recommend to people who hate crowded beaches. Over a kilometre of sand, multiple surf peaks that spread the crowd, and the one thing no other popular Algarve beach can offer: guaranteed parking. Even on the busiest summer weekend, you'll find a spot. The main peaks are in front of the car park — walk further for emptier waves. If the wind ruins Cordoama, neighbouring Castelejo in its sheltered cove is often perfectly clean.
beaches.skipIf: You want calm swimming — this is a surf beach with serious Atlantic current. Non-surfers can still enjoy the walk, the drama, and the beach restaurant, but the water is for strong swimmers only.

beaches.name: Praia do Amado
beaches.vibeLine: The Algarve's most consistent surf break. Waves year-round, red-ochre cliffs, and an energy that's hard to explain until you feel it.
beaches.bestTime: Arrive before 10am in summer — the parking fills with cars and campervans. Spring and autumn offer the best balance of good waves and manageable crowds. Winter brings head-high+ swells for experienced surfers only.
beaches.parking: Two large lots directly above the beach. Free but fills early in summer. Paved road suitable for campervans.
beaches.personalTake: Even if you don't surf, Amado is worth the drive. The wide bay framed by red-ochre cliffs hosts international competitions for a reason — the waves just keep coming. Grab a beer from the snack bar, sit on the cliff, and watch the sunset with the surfers. If you do want to try, Amado Surf Camp is run by local natives who know these waters better than anyone. Nearby Praia da Bordeira offers similar quality with fewer people if Amado feels busy.
beaches.skipIf: You want to swim casually — the currents are strong and the water is cold (wetsuit territory year-round). Winter waves can exceed 10ft — know your limits.

beaches.name: Praia do Beliche
beaches.vibeLine: 100 steep steps down to the 'end of the world' — dramatic cliffs, powerful waves, and a vibe that rewards commitment.
beaches.bestTime: Always check conditions from the clifftop before committing to the descent. Avoid low tide — waves get dumpy and dangerous. Works when Tonel is blown out because the 40m cliffs block north/northeast winds.
beaches.parking: Free gravel lot by the road. Limited spaces — fills quickly during good swells. No alternatives.
beaches.personalTake: Beliche is the Algarve's only proper wedge wave — powerful, hollow barrels breaking over shallow water. It's not for beginners, and the 100-step descent is the beach's way of asking if you're serious. But the reward is a golden cove at the base of 40-metre cliffs between Sagres and Cape St. Vincent, where the sunset views are worth the climb back up even if you never touch the water. The restaurant at the top is a welcome sight after those stairs.
beaches.skipIf: You're not a confident swimmer or surfer — the waves are genuinely powerful. Mobility issues make the 100 steep stone steps a dealbreaker. Allow 15 minutes for the climb back up.

beaches.name: Praia do Telheiro
beaches.vibeLine: Wild, remote, and home to one of Europe's most important geological formations. The walk down is an adventure in itself.
beaches.bestTime: Allow 3+ hours for a proper visit including the 15-20 minute walk each way. Any time of day works — you'll almost certainly be alone. Spring and autumn for hiking; autumn for surf.
beaches.parking: Free parking at the trailhead. Space for 15-20 cars — usually more than enough because almost nobody comes here.
beaches.personalTake: Telheiro is for people who want to earn their beach. The steep, rocky 20-minute descent weeds out the casual visitors, and what's left is raw Algarve — towering cliffs with a geological unconformity that scientists travel to study, powerful surf, and complete solitude. Bring proper hiking boots, pack everything you need (including plenty of water), and give yourself time. The Rota Vicentina Fisherman's Trail passes above — combine it for a proper coastal adventure.
beaches.skipIf: You want easy access, facilities, or calm swimming. The path is steep and rocky. This is a commitment beach — and it should be.

beaches.name: Praia da Marinha
beaches.vibeLine: Consistently rated one of Europe's most beautiful beaches — and for once, the hype is justified.
beaches.bestTime: Before 9am or after 5pm. The midday crush is brutal in summer — tour buses arrive from 10am and the magic disappears under umbrellas and selfie sticks. Low tide is essential for walking close to the famous double arch.
beaches.parking: Large lot (€2/day) — a bargain for what you get. Fills by 9:30am in summer.
beaches.personalTake: Yes, it's famous. Yes, it's on every Instagram. And yes, it genuinely deserves it. The double arch formation is more dramatic in person than any photo suggests, and the crystal-clear water is some of the best swimming in the Algarve. The secret is timing — come at 7am or at sunset and you'll understand why this beach has every award. May-June is the sweet spot: warm, swimmable, and the summer hordes haven't arrived. Combine with Benagil Cave (10 minutes drive) for the best morning on the coast.
beaches.skipIf: You can only visit between 10am-4pm in July/August — you'll share it with hundreds of people and wonder what the fuss is about. That's not Marinha's fault.

beaches.name: Praia de Benagil
beaches.vibeLine: Portugal's most famous sea cave with its iconic skylight. The beach is tiny — the cave is everything.
beaches.bestTime: Book a 7:30am kayak tour. Yes, they exist. You'll have the cave nearly to yourself, the light is better for photos, and the sea is calmer. The 10am-4pm window is chaos — 50+ boats circling, 20-minute waits, and photos full of kayaks instead of cave.
beaches.parking: Limited lot (€5/day). Fills by 9am in peak season. If it's full, you're already too late for the good experience anyway.
beaches.personalTake: The cave is genuinely magical — the skylight creates a cathedral of light on the sand inside. But the experience is entirely defined by when you go. Early morning or off-season (November-March, tours still run on good weather days) and you might be the only boat there. Midday in August and you'll queue with 200 other people wondering why you bothered. Book kayak tours at least a week ahead in summer — they sell out. This is the single best timing hack in the entire guide.
beaches.skipIf: You can only go mid-morning in summer and expect a peaceful experience. Also: the beach itself is tiny and not great for spending the day. Come for the cave, then move on.

beaches.name: Ilha de Tavira
beaches.vibeLine: A barrier island beach that stretches for kilometres — warm, shallow, and the eastern Algarve's answer to the western cliffs. Different beauty, equal magic.
beaches.bestTime: The ferry from Tavira runs every 15-30 minutes in summer (€2 return). The beach near the ferry landing is busy — walk 10 minutes east and the crowd thins dramatically. September is perfect: warm water, quiet beaches, golden light.
beaches.parking: Park in Tavira town (near the ferry terminal) or at the Quatro Águas pier. Both are manageable outside peak summer weekends.
beaches.personalTake: People fixated on the western Algarve's cliffs miss the eastern coast entirely — and Ilha de Tavira is the best argument for why that's a mistake. The water is warmer, the sand is wider, and the Ria Formosa lagoon behind you is teeming with birdlife. The western end has a popular naturist section. The real move: bring a picnic, walk past the restaurants, and find your own stretch. At sunset, the light across the lagoon is photographer's gold.
beaches.skipIf: You want dramatic cliffs and coves — this is flat, wide, and sandy. You don't want to rely on ferry schedules (last ferry back is around 7-8pm in summer, earlier off-season).

beaches.name: Praia do Tonel
beaches.vibeLine: Where a 15th-century fortress meets surf culture at the edge of Europe. Sunsets here feel like the end of the world — because it nearly is.
beaches.bestTime: Early morning for surf (before the wind picks up). Sunset is the real event — the fortress silhouette against the orange sky is unforgettable. Summer has full facilities; winter you're on your own.
beaches.parking: Free parking behind the beach. If full, use the larger Sagres Fortress car park (300m walk) — it always has space.
beaches.personalTake: Tonel is my favourite sunset beach in the Algarve, and it's not even close. The Sagres Fortress looming above, the Atlantic stretching to infinity, and the sense that you're standing at the very edge of the continent — it all comes together in the last hour of daylight. During the day it's a solid surf beach with a seasonal bar, but the magic is at golden hour. Wetsuit recommended year-round — this is cold Atlantic water, not the warm south coast.
beaches.skipIf: You want calm, warm swimming water — Tonel is west-facing Atlantic with cold currents and surf. The beach bar and facilities are summer-only.

beaches.name: Ilha Deserta
beaches.vibeLine: Portugal's southernmost point. Seven kilometres of white sand, one restaurant, zero buildings. A desert island that's actually real.
beaches.bestTime: September-October is perfect — warm water, no queues for the ferry, and the one restaurant isn't fully booked. Summer means ferry queues and booking O Estamine ahead. The ferry itself (€10 return from Faro) is scenic — keep your camera ready.
beaches.parking: Park at Faro's Porta Nova pier (paid) or nearby streets. Ferry departs from Cais da Porta Nova (45 min journey, or €20 speedboat for 15 min).
beaches.personalTake: This is the beach I save for people who think they've seen everything the Algarve has to offer. Seven kilometres of pristine sand on an uninhabited barrier island with one restaurant and 300 species of birds. Walk 20 minutes from the ferry landing and it's just you and the ocean. There is zero shade on the entire island — bring a parasol or suffer. Book lunch at O Estamine in advance during summer — it's the only place to eat and it's actually very good. The western section is officially naturist if that's your thing.
beaches.skipIf: You forgot sunscreen, a parasol, and water. Seriously — there's no shade anywhere on the island. Also not ideal if you need regular facilities or don't want to commit to ferry schedules.
